entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 0: The big picture
entry.content:
Part 0 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent. This post is the map; Parts 1 to 7 build it, one piece at a time.

Moving integration content from a development system to the next system sounds simple. In SAP BTP it takes three services, five connections and three kinds of permissions. In my last project, connecting the services took a few hours. Getting the permissions right took days.

This series walks through the setup I built, in plain words. This first post explains the pieces, how they fit together, and the one idea that would have saved me most of those days.

What we move

  • Integration Suite packages: your integration flows and everything that belongs to them.
  • Role collections: bundles of permissions you give to users.
  • Destinations: saved connection details (an address plus how to log in).

The three services, in one sentence each

Think of a transport as sending a parcel.

  • SAP Integration Suite is where developers build. It has a Transport button. That is where the parcel starts.
  • SAP Content Agent service is the packer. It collects the content and packs it into one file, an MTA archive (.mtar). On the other side, a second Content Agent unpacks it.
  • SAP Cloud Transport Management (CTMS) is the delivery service. It never opens the parcel. It moves it from one stop (a node) to the next along a route, and a person with the right permission decides when it is delivered (the import).

The landscape

Everything runs between two subaccounts, and the whole series stays with these two:

  • Dev: where developers build and click Transport.
  • Central: holds the one CTMS for the whole landscape, and the target Integration Suite.

 

 

The five steps in the picture are the whole journey. A developer clicks Transport (1), Content Agent packs the parcel (2), CTMS delivers it (3), someone approves the import (4), and the second Content Agent unpacks it into the target (5).

SAP's tutorials put CTMS in the development subaccount. We put it in Central, so every environment shares one delivery service and Dev only needs a connection to it.

The connections: destinations

Every arrow in the picture is a destination: a saved address plus login details, copied from a service key (the credentials a service gives you). Three of them must have exact names, because Integration Suite looks them up by name: ContentAssemblyService, CloudIntegration and TransportManagementService. Parts 2 and 3 set them up field by field.

The first sign that they work is the Transport setting in Integration Suite:

 

 

The one idea: who is asking?

Almost every error I hit came from giving a permission to the wrong "who". Before you assign anything, ask: is this a service talking to another service, or a person clicking in a screen?

Who is askingWhat it needsWhere you set itWhat you see when it is missing
A service, calling another serviceRoles on the service instanceWhen you create or update the instanceThe transport stops half-way
A person, in a browserA role collection on their userSecurity > Role CollectionsA button or tile is missing
The connection between themA destination with the right credentialsConnectivity > Destinations"Failed to fetch auth token" or "not connected"

Two rules follow from this:

  • A role collection does nothing for a service, and an instance role does nothing for a person.
  • A destination is only as good as the key it was copied from. A wrong client ID or token URL fails quietly until you run a real transport.

Here is what a destination problem looks like. The setting is saved, but the check fails because one destination cannot log in:

 

 

The exact roles are introduced in the part where you need them, and Part 7 collects all of them on one page.

What does not travel

The parcel carries definitions, not secrets. After every import you set these in the target yourself:

  • passwords and client secrets of transported destinations,
  • which users get which role collections,
  • security material (keys and credentials) and values that differ per environment.

The series

PartTopic
0The big picture (this post)
1Central: setting up CTMS, its nodes and the route
2Dev: Content Agent and the three fixed-name destinations
3Central: the second Content Agent and the target
4Switching on Transport and running the first one
5Transporting role collections
6Transporting destinations
7Cheat sheet: every role, where it goes, what breaks without it

Alongside the parts I will publish short Troubleshooting posts, one per error I hit, each linked from the part where it shows up. Links are added here as posts go live.

Before you start

  • Two subaccounts in the Cloud Foundry environment: one for Dev, one for Central.
  • SAP Integration Suite in both, with the Cloud Integration capability switched on.
  • Entitlements for Cloud Transport Management, Content Agent service, Process Integration Runtime and Authorization and Trust Management.
  • Administrator access to both subaccounts.

What comes next. In Part 1 we set up the delivery service, CTMS, in the Central subaccount: subscribing to it, creating the service instance and key, building the source and target nodes, and connecting them with a route. By the end of Part 1 you will have an empty but working transport route, ready for Content Agent to send its first parcel in Part 2.

Does your landscape look different, for example with CTMS in the development subaccount? Tell me in the comments.

entry.title: Building an MCP Server for SAP S/4HANA on SAP BTP
entry.content:
Introduction

Consider a routine business question: "How many sales orders did this customer place this year?" The answer already exists in SAP S/4HANA, yet obtaining it typically involves opening the right application, setting filters, exporting a list and counting the rows. The data is available, but the path to it is designed for experienced SAP users.

The solution described in this article provides a simpler path: a question goes in, and the answer comes straight from the system. Rather than adding another point-to-point integration, it places a single, well-defined layer in front of SAP S/4HANA: an MCP server. The server offers a small set of clearly described, read-only tools (count sales orders, find a business partner, show a cost center) and performs all SAP communication itself, using only released OData APIs and standard SAP BTP connectivity.

In the current implementation, a chat application calls these tools through a built-in, rule-based mode. No language model is involved, and every answer is built directly from SAP data.

All configuration is described generically. No system names, URLs, client numbers, IDs or credentials are included, so the approach can be mapped onto any landscape.

MCP at a Glance

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting applications to tools and data. An MCP server publishes a list of tools, each with a name, a description and parameters. A client (a chat application, an assistant or an agent platform) picks the right tool for a question, calls it and shows the result.

For SAP, this means the SAP logic is built once, in one governed place, and any MCP-capable client can reuse it. Clients can only call what the server publishes, nothing more.

Solution Architecture

No client communicates with SAP S/4HANA directly. Clients only call tools on the MCP server, and the server reaches the backend through standard SAP BTP services.

The client calls the MCP server; the server resolves the target system through the Destination service and reaches it through the Connectivity service and the Cloud Connector.

Layer Component Responsibility

ClientChat application (or any MCP client)Receives the question, selects a tool, presents the answer
ToolsMCP server (Python application)Offers S/4HANA data as read-only tools
RuntimeSAP BTP, Cloud FoundryHosts the MCP server
ConfigurationDestination serviceStores the target system's address and logon, outside the code
NetworkConnectivity service + Cloud ConnectorSecurely tunnels requests from SAP BTP into the on-premise network
BackendSAP S/4HANAProvides data through released OData V2 APIs

Connectivity to SAP S/4HANA

On SAP BTP, the MCP server reaches SAP S/4HANA in the standard way: it reads the target system from a destination, and every request travels through the Connectivity service and the Cloud Connector into the on-premise network. The server holds no SAP host names or passwords; both live in the destination.

For local development, the same server can call a test system directly with a technical user over VPN. No code change is needed to switch between the two.

Cloud Connector Configuration

One system mapping is sufficient. Exposing only the OData path keeps every other path on the system unreachable from SAP BTP.

Setting Value

Back-end typeABAP System
ProtocolHTTPS
Internal host / port<S/4HANA host> / <HTTPS port>
Virtual host / port<virtual host> / <virtual port>
Resource (URL path)/sap/opu/odata/ with "Path and all sub-paths"

Destination Configuration

The destination is created once in the SAP BTP cockpit (Connectivity → Destinations). A password change for the technical user is made here and requires no redeployment.

Field Value

Name<destination name>
TypeHTTP
URLhttp://<virtual host>:<virtual port>
Proxy TypeOnPremise
AuthenticationBasicAuthentication (technical user with read authorizations)
Additional propertysap-client = <client>
Location IDOnly if the Cloud Connector uses one

Request Flow

  1. A client calls a tool on the MCP server.
  2. The server reads the destination (cached for a few minutes) to learn where the system is and how to log on.
  3. The request goes through the Connectivity service and the Cloud Connector to SAP S/4HANA.
  4. SAP returns the data through the released OData API, and the server passes a clean result back to the client.

Tool Design

Clients choose tools by their names and descriptions, so these are written as carefully as the logic behind them.

Business-Specific Tools

The most frequent questions have their own tools:

  • Business partners: search by name, count, show details and addresses.
  • Sales orders: list, count, show one order with its items.
  • Cost centers: search, count, show details, and actual costs per G/L account or period.

Three rules apply to all of them:

  • Counts come from SAP. "How many…?" questions use dedicated count tools that ask SAP for the exact total instead of downloading and counting rows.
  • Lists always state the real total. A list shows at most a few hundred rows, but always begins with "Total in SAP: N (showing M)", so a shortened list is never mistaken for the full result.
  • Nothing is assumed. Values such as the leading ledger or the current fiscal year are read from SAP at runtime, and IDs are always looked up, never guessed.

Generic Discovery Tools

For everything else, three read-only tools work on any allowed OData service:

  • List services: which SAP APIs may be used.
  • Describe a service: its entity sets and fields, with SAP's own field labels (read from $metadata).
  • Query a service: read rows with filters, always with the total number of matches.

Natural-Language Search Based on SAP Metadata

For questions that no specific tool covers, a search tool takes the question as plain text and works out the query on its own. It contains no hard-coded list of services or fields. Instead, it reads the metadata of every allowed service and matches the words in the question against SAP's own entity and field labels. For example, "maintenance notifications for plant 1000" is matched to the maintenance notification entity set, with a filter on the plant field.

Every result states exactly what was queried: service, entity set and filter. If the search picks the wrong data, the user can see why and rephrase. The search is deliberately simple, covering one entity set at a time with counts, filters, text search and sorting by latest or largest.

Service Governance and Allow-List

The generic tools work only on an allow-list of OData services. A default list is defined in the code, and two settings on the application change it without redeployment:

  • SAP_ALLOWED_SERVICES replaces the list.
  • SAP_EXTRA_SERVICES adds services to it.

The list was chosen with the help of a small inventory script. It reads the system's own service catalog (/IWFND/CATALOGSERVICE), classifies every registered service as standard API, custom or other, and checks for each candidate whether its metadata responds and whether the technical user can read data. The result is a list of service names only, with no business data, which gives the SAP Basis team a clear, factual view of what is active, what fails and what is not available in the installed release.

The server also checks this catalog regularly and hides any tool whose service is not registered in the system. Once SAP Basis activates a service, its tools appear automatically, without a code change.

What SAP Basis Needs to Provide

Item Where

Cloud Connector connected to the subaccount, with the OData path exposedCloud Connector administration
A technical user with read authorizations: S_SERVICE for each allowed OData service, plus the business authorizations for the dataSU01 / PFCG
The required OData services activated/IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE
Analysis of failing services (HTTP 500 and similar)/IWFND/ERROR_LOG
Later, for production: principal propagation, so each user sees only data their own SAP authorizations allowCloud Connector and SAP S/4HANA trust configuration

Deployment Steps

1. Implement the MCP Tools

The server is a small Python application built with the official MCP SDK. A tool is an ordinary function marked with @McP.tool():

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("S4HANA Server")

@mcp.tool()
async def count_sales_orders(customer: str = "") -> str:
    """Exact NUMBER of SAP sales orders. Give 'customer' (sold-to party) to count only theirs."""
    flt = f"SoldToParty eq '{customer}'" if customer else ""
    total = await sap_count("API_SALES_ORDER_SRV", "A_SalesOrder", flt)
    return f"Count of sales orders: {total}"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mcp.run(transport="streamable-http")
  • The docstring becomes the tool description that clients read to decide when to use it.
  • The parameters (here customer) become the tool's input schema.
  • sap_count is a small helper that calls the OData service through the destination and asks SAP only for the total ($inlinecount=allpages with $top=1), so no rows are downloaded.
  • mcp.run starts the server over HTTP, which is how it runs on SAP BTP. For local testing it can run over standard input/output instead.
pip install "mcp[cli]" httpx

2. Create the BTP Service Instances

cf create-service destination lite <destination-instance>
cf create-service connectivity lite <connectivity-instance>
cf cups <secrets-instance> -p secrets.json      # holds the MCP access key; delete the file afterwards

3. Describe the Application

A short manifest.yml binds the three services and keeps writes switched off:

applications:
  - name: <mcp-app>
    buildpacks: [python_buildpack]
    memory: 256M
    command: python server.py
    services: [<destination-instance>, <connectivity-instance>, <secrets-instance>]
    env:
      MCP_TRANSPORT: http
      SAP_ALLOW_WRITES: "false"

4. Deploy

The destination name is set once as an application setting, so the repository contains no system-specific values:

cf login -a https://api.cf.<region>.hana.ondemand.com --sso
cf set-env <mcp-app> SAP_DESTINATION <destination-name>   # once
cf push
cf logs <mcp-app> --recent

5. Verify

Before connecting the chat application, a test client lists the tools on the deployed server and runs each one against real data. Tools whose services are not activated should not appear in the list.

Challenges and Resolutions

Challenge Root cause Resolution

"403 – No service found" for a standard APIThe service was not activated, or it was registered under a different technical name than its URL nameCall services by the URL name shown in the service catalog; activate missing services in /IWFND/MAINT_SERVICE
HTTP 406 when reading service metadataMetadata is only available as XML, but JSON was requestedRequest metadata as XML
HTTP 400 on certain analytical entity setsThese entity sets require mandatory parametersExclude them from the generic search; query them with their parameters
HTTP 500 on individual servicesService-side errors in the backendAnalysed by SAP Basis in /IWFND/ERROR_LOG
Empty results for some queriesMissing authorizations for the technical userCheck read access per service early with the inventory script
Errors on open-ended "valid to 9999-12-31" datesDate conversion overflow in the applicationFixed in the server's date handling
Slow responsesThe destination was read on every callCache the destination for a few minutes

Key Takeaways

  • MCP provides a clean integration layer for SAP: build the S/4HANA access once and reuse it from any MCP-capable client.
  • Clean core is maintained: released OData APIs, the Destination and Connectivity services and the Cloud Connector keep the solution upgrade-safe and easy to approve.
  • Access is governed through configuration: an allow-list, checked against the system's own catalog, exposes only what exists and what is permitted.
  • Read-only comes first: accurate answers build trust before any write scenario is considered.

Conclusion

Making SAP S/4HANA data accessible through simple questions requires neither replacing existing systems nor modifying the core. An MCP server in front of standard OData APIs, running on SAP BTP with standard connectivity, turns the system of record into a set of secure, well-described tools. Every figure in an answer comes directly from SAP.

The lasting value is a reusable integration layer: today a chat application uses it directly, and other MCP-capable clients can use the same layer tomorrow without any change on the SAP side.

Feedback and experiences from similar SAP S/4HANA integrations are welcome in the comments.

entry.title: AI-Assisted Solution Blueprint Proposal Feature on SAP Discovery Center: Join the Beta Program
entry.content:
SAP's AI solution portfolio is expanding at an extraordinary pace - spanning Cloud ERP, Industry AI, and SAP Business AI Platform, with SAP and its partners continuously delivering new AI features, Joule agents and Joule assistants. To help you navigate this expanding landscape with speed and confidence, SAP is looking to introduce an AI-assisted solution blueprint proposal feature on SAP Discovery Center. This AI feature takes you from a natural-language business problem statement to a selection of solution options to choose from, up to a structured solution blueprint, in a fraction of the time it would take through manual discovery.

What is this AI feature all about?

The AI-assisted solution blueprint proposal feature is an AI-driven capability that enables business-led discovery of the best-fitting AI solutions - from SAP, SAP partners and custom built - for any business challenge. Rather than manually browsing catalogs or relying on specialist engagement to arrive at an initial design, this feature guides you from a natural-language problem statement to a structured solution blueprint.

The AI feature is built on SAP Business AI Platform and is planned to be delivered through SAP Discovery Center, SAP's central platform for discovering, evaluating, and adopting ready-to-use AI solutions and SAP Business AI Platform.

How it works

The AI-assisted solution blueprint proposal feature works as follows:

  • Step 1 - Describe your business needs: You enter your requirements in natural language.
    Describe Business Need
  • Step 2 - Review business details: Th AI feature analyses your input, provides tips to improve your results and asks you to review the adapted requirement description.
    Review Business Details
  • Step 3 - Select solution proposal: The AI feature proposes solution options by matching your requirements against the functional scope of AI solutions (e.g. Joule assistants, Joule agents and AI features) from SAP and SAP partners and custom-built solutions on SAP Business AI Platform. As a result, a list of solution options - single or multi-product - is provided which are ranked by fit to the stated requirements. For each solution option detailed scores including supporting explanations are available.
    Select Solution Proposal
    When choosing a custom solution option, you will get an adaptable solution diagram, list of required and optional SAP Business AI Platform solutions, including a summary and explanation of the architecture:
    Custom Solution Architecture

Why this matters for you

This feature shortens the cycle from business need through solution discovery to the actual solution blueprint significantly. Crucially, it is grounded in proprietary SAP product knowledge, so the recommendations it surfaces are aligned with the actual capabilities of SAP's solution portfolio.

Want to try it out?

Join the beta program for the AI-assisted solution blueprint proposal feature on SAP Discovery Center. Registration is open now through November 6, 2026. To sign up, visit the beta program page on SAP Customer Influence & Adoption and follow the registration instructions. Once your participation will have been confirmed you will get access to the AI-assisted solution blueprint proposal feature on SAP Discovery Center to try it out. Help us to further improve and evolve the new feature by joining a feedback session and participating the feedback survey as part of the beta program activities.

entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 1: Setting up CTMS in Central
entry.content:
Part 1 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 0 we drew the map: Content Agent packs the parcel, CTMS delivers it, a second Content Agent unpacks it. In this part we build the delivery service itself: CTMS in the Central subaccount, with two stops (nodes) and the road between them (a route).

 

Step 1: Subscribe to CTMS

In the Central subaccount, go to Services > Service Marketplace, find Cloud Transport Management and create a subscription. The subscription is the screen people work in.

Then, in Security > Role Collections, create a role collection with the CTMS role Administrator and assign it to your user. Without it the app may open, but you cannot create nodes or routes.

Step 2: Create a service instance and a key

The subscription is for people. Other services need their own door. In the same subaccount, create a service instance of Cloud Transport Management with plan standard, then create a service key on it.

The key holds four values we need later: the address (uri), the login (clientid and clientsecret) and the token server (uaa.url). In Part 2 these go into the Dev destination TransportManagementService.

Treat the key like a password. Do not paste it in tickets or screenshots.

Step 3: Create the source node

Open the CTMS app, go to Transport Nodes and click +.

  • Name: something clear, for example SOURCE_NODE. Write it down: Part 2 uses this exact name.
  • Tick Allow Upload to Node. This lets Content Agent in Dev drop parcels here.
  • Leave content type and destination empty. Nothing is ever imported into a source node.

Step 4: Create the target node

  • Name: for example TARGET_NODE.
  • Content Type: Multi-Target Application. That is the parcel format Content Agent produces.
  • Destination: leave it empty for now. Part 3 creates CAS_on_Target, the connection to the Content Agent that unpacks the parcel, and we come back to fill it in.
  • Forward Mode: keep the default. It only matters when there is another node after this one.

Step 5: Create the route

Go to Transport Routes, click +, give it a name, pick the source node and the target node, and save. That is all a route is: "parcels from here go there".

 

Left: creating a node (names blurred). Right: creating the route.

Check it

Open Landscape Visualization. You should see two boxes joined by an arrow. If the arrow is missing, the route was not saved with both nodes.

Roles for this part

WhoNeedsFor
You, building the landscapeCTMS role Administrator, in a role collectionCreating nodes and routes
Whoever imports laterCTMS role ImportOperator, in a role collectionClicking Import on the target node (Part 4)

The full list for every service is in Part 7.

What tripped me up in my setup

These are from my own project log, not from the documentation.

  • The cockpit shortcut does not work across subaccounts. The key lives in Central, but the destination that uses it (Part 2) lives in Dev. The "Create from Service Instance" option on the Destinations screen only sees keys in its own subaccount, so I had to copy the values from the key by hand.
  • That hand copy caused my first real error. The client ID in my destination did not match the key, and Content Agent could not reach CTMS until I copied it again. My advice: create a fresh key and copy all four values from it in one go, never from an older key or a note.
  • Old instances cost me time. Earlier tutorial attempts had left two CTMS instances (and several other duplicates in different spaces) in my landscape, and I had to work out which key belonged to which. Keep one CTMS instance per landscape, give it a clear name, and note which space it is in.
  • Choose the source node name once. Part 2 needs it character for character, so decide the final name before you create the node.

What comes next

CTMS is ready but empty. In Part 2 we switch to the Dev subaccount, set up Content Agent and create the three fixed-name destinations, using the service key from step 2 and the source node name from step 3.

entry.title: SAP Green Ledger: Q3-26 Release Updates and Highlights
entry.content:
Welcome to the Q3 2026 edition of our SAP Green Ledger Quarterly Release Highlights! This blog summarizes the most important innovations and enhancements delivered for SAP Green Ledger during Q3 2026.

This quarter brought several new capabilities and enhancements to SAP Green Ledger, including faster master data imports with delta loads, new APIs for integrating carbon data from external sources, carbon allocations from energy flows, and more flexible GHG analysis. Further enhancements improve CBAM liability management and usability.

Read on to learn more about the key innovations introduced throughout Q3 2026: 

  • Faster Master Data Imports with Delta Loads 
  • API-Based Carbon Data Imports 
  • Enhanced Carbon Data Import Details
  • Carbon Allocations from Energy Flows
  • WBS Elements for Manual Journal Entries 
  • Enhanced Carbon Liability Management 
  • More Flexible GHG Analysis in the Carbon Data Dashboard 
  • Enhanced Carbon and Financial Analysis in the Analytical Dashboard 
  • Further Updates and Enhancements

 

Faster Master Data Imports with Delta Loads

The Manage Master Data Imports app now supports delta loads in addition to full loads when importing master data from a connected SAP S/4HANA system, enabling faster and more efficient master data imports. Instead of importing the complete master data scope with every import, a delta load imports only newly created and changed master data objects since the previous full or delta load. This reduces the amount of data that needs to be processed and can significantly shorten the time required for the import.

Delta Load Option for Master Data Import from Connected SAP S/4HANA System

Delta loads are currently supported for account, account hierarchy, product, and project master data in both SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition. For cost center master data, delta loads are currently supported for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. Other master data objects continue to be imported in full, even when the import is started as a delta load. The first master data import is always performed as a full load. A full load may also be required for subsequent imports, for example when changes are made to the relevant business system.

For more information, see SAP Help: Import Master Data.

 

API-Based Carbon Data Imports

SAP Green Ledger now provides three APIs for importing and processing carbon data from external sources. In addition to importing emission data from external sources via CSV files, the new APIs now provide a defined interface for integrating this data into SAP Green Ledger. The APIs support the different steps of the carbon data import process, from importing carbon data to releasing an import and monitoring its processing status.

The Carbon Data Import API allows you to import carbon data and create the data for the corresponding carbon collections. The Carbon Data Import Release API can then be used to release an import and trigger the creation of the corresponding carbon collections and journal entries. To monitor the process, the Carbon Data Import Status API provides information about the status of an import and the processing results of the corresponding carbon collections.

For more information, see the API Guide for SAP Green Ledger.

 

Enhanced Carbon Data Import Details

Once carbon data has been imported into SAP Green Ledger, it is important to understand how the data has been processed and what resulted from the import.

The Manage Carbon Data Imports app now provides more detailed information about your carbon data imports. You can review the imported data as well as the carbon collections and journal entries created from an import and navigate between them. This provides greater transparency into the results of a carbon data import and makes it easier to trace the imported data through to the resulting carbon collections and journal entries. The enhanced overview and navigation are available for new carbon data imports; existing imports remain unchanged.

For more information, see SAP Help: Import Material Movements.

 

Carbon Allocations from Energy Flows

Energy flow models in SAP Sustainability Footprint Management represent how energy and the associated emissions are distributed across different elements of an organization. SAP Green Ledger now brings this information into carbon accounting to reflect the corresponding carbon allocations between cost centers. To support this, the import of modeled energy flows from SAP Sustainability Footprint Management has been extended. In addition to carbon emissions for energy sources, emissions for other nodes in the energy flow, such as facilities, meters, resources, and process infrastructures, are now also imported.

Using the Manage Carbon Data Imports app, you can import and release energy flows from a connected SAP Sustainability Footprint Management system. The imported data includes the cost center assignments of the individual nodes, which are carried into the corresponding carbon collections. When these carbon collections are posted to the journal, SAP Green Ledger creates the corresponding cost center-to-cost center allocations based on the modeled energy flow. The resulting journal entries include the respective cost centers and partner cost centers.

The carbon collections and resulting journal entries can be reviewed in the Manage Carbon Collections and Manage Journal Entries apps.

For more information, see SAP Help: Import Energy Flows.

 

WBS Elements for Manual Journal Entries

Carbon adjustments and corrections can now also be assigned to specific WBS elements when journal entries are created manually. The Manage Journal Entries app now supports WBS elements and partner WBS elements for manual journal entries.

When creating a manual journal entry, you can now assign a WBS element to a line item for eligible accounts. Cost center and WBS element are mutually exclusive and cannot be maintained for the same line item. When a WBS element is selected, the corresponding profit center and segment are automatically derived.

The WBS element value help displays WBS elements based on the relevant project and profit center context. The system also checks whether the selected WBS element is available for posting and informs you if any posting restrictions apply.

For more information, see SAP Help: Create Journal Entries.

 

Enhanced Carbon Liability Management

With the EU CBAM definitive regime in effect since January 2026, imports of certain goods into the European Union can result in carbon liabilities that need to be recognized and valued. SAP Green Ledger supports this process by accounting for the embedded emissions and the resulting carbon liabilities and by determining their fair value based on the corresponding certificate requirements and Emissions Trading System (ETS) prices. In Q3 2026, new enhancements provide further support for the valuation and review of these liabilities.

Official EU ETS Prices

The Configure Carbon Certificate Data app now displays the official quarterly ETS prices published by the European Union. These prices are automatically imported into SAP Green Ledger and used for the fair value calculation of carbon liabilities associated with imports subject to EU CBAM. You can view the official quarterly prices together with your maintained ETS prices in the Emissions Trading System Prices tab.

Official EU ETS Prices Imported for Quarter 1 and 2

A color indicator shows whether ETS prices are available for the current year and quarter: green indicates that prices are maintained for all calendar weeks, while blue indicates that the automatically imported official quarterly EU ETS prices are used.

For more information, see SAP Help: View and Maintain Emissions Trading System Prices.

Product Information in Carbon Liabilities

The Manage Carbon Liabilities app now displays the Product selected for carbon collections that require carbon certificates, providing additional context when reviewing carbon liabilities.

For more information, see SAP Help: View Carbon Liabilities and Create a Carbon Collection.

 

More Flexible GHG Analysis in the Carbon Data Dashboard 

The Carbon Data Dashboard has been enhanced with new options for analyzing GHG emissions. 

The timing of GHG emission recognition can differ depending on whether emissions are considered when carbon data is posted or when the underlying resources are actually consumed. You can now choose between the accrual and non-accrual accounting method, which determines how GHG emissions are calculated and displayed in the dashboard. 

With the non-accrual method, GHG emissions are recognized when carbon-relevant data is posted to the GHG Liabilities Collection account. The resulting GHG emissions therefore represent the emissions recorded at the time of the carbon data posting, regardless of subsequent activities related to the underlying resources. 

With the accrual method, emissions are distinguished based on whether the underlying resources have already been consumed. Emissions related to consumed resources are recognized as realized GHG emissions in profit and loss accounts, while emissions related to resources that have not yet been consumed remain as accrued emissions in balance sheet accounts. As the resources are consumed, the corresponding emissions move from the balance sheet to profit and loss. This allows the dashboard to reflect GHG emissions in line with actual resource consumption.

Selection of Accrued and Non-Accrued GHG Emissions Overview

The Carbon Data Dashboard also introduces an enhancement to the WBS Element filter. The filter is now organized by project, with a project node at the top of the hierarchy grouping the corresponding WBS elements. This provides clearer context and makes it easier to locate and select WBS elements within their associated projects.

Enhanced WBS Element Filter Organized by Project

 For more information, see SAP Help: Analyze Carbon Data and Accounting Method.

 

Enhanced Carbon and Financial Analysis in the Analytical Dashboard 

The SAP Green Ledger Analytical Dashboard has also been updated for Q3 2026 with enhancements to filtering and data visualization. The updates make it easier to analyze carbon data in the context of projects and WBS elements and further improve the presentation and interpretation of GHG and financial data. 

For a detailed overview of the latest SAP Green Ledger Analytical Dashboard enhancements, see the dedicated SAP Community blog post and the SAP Help Portal topic Analyze Carbon Data Alongside Financial Data.

 

Further Updates and Enhancements

Several smaller enhancements further improve the usability of SAP Green Ledger. 

Line Item Totals and Subtotals 

The Line Items table in the Manage Journal Entries app now displays debit and credit totals and subtotals. When line items are grouped by an attribute, you can view the corresponding subtotals for each group, making it easier to analyze and review carbon-related postings. 

Filtering by Empty Dimension Values 

The Manage Journal Entries, Display Line Items, and Display Account Balances apps now allow you to filter for empty or unassigned values across supported dimensions, including, for example, WBS element, cost center, product, and supplier. You can display only postings where a particular dimension has not been assigned, or exclude these postings from the results. This makes it easier to review postings based on whether specific dimension information is available. 

Journal Entry IDs Without Leading Zeros 

Journal entry IDs are now displayed without leading zeros across SAP Green Ledger, making them easier to read, search, and sort. This applies wherever journal entry IDs are displayed. 

Documentation Feedback on SAP Help Portal

You can now provide feedback directly on the Admin Guide, Integration Guide, API Guide, and Introduction for SAP Green Ledger on SAP Help Portal. This makes it easier to share feedback on specific documentation content directly from the page you are viewing. For more information, see SAP Help: Giving Documentation Feedback on SAP Help Portal.

 

Additional Information 

If you want to dive deeper into SAP Green Ledger, the SAP Help Portal is a good place to start. It provides detailed information on concepts, configuration, and application usage. You can also check the What’s New section, which is updated with every release and gives a complete overview of the latest additions. To see what's coming next, the SAP Road Map Explorer offers insight into planned features and upcoming innovations. It is updated regularly and outlines how the solution will continue to evolve.

entry.title: Several e-mail addresses, one SAP user: CERTRULE instead of the gateway mapping table for BTP apps
entry.content:
INTRODUCTION

This blog is on a challenge we faced with principal propagation from SAP BTP to an on-premise ABAP system through the Cloud Connector. With principal propagation a user logs on to an app on SAP BTP and the call that app makes to the ABAP system runs as that same person without a technical user and without a second password.

It describes the solution to a problem we met while moving from SAP ECC to S/4HANA. In ECC, our BTP apps reach the back end through a gateway system and the gateway finds the SAP user behind a call through the external ID mapping table USREXTID (view VUSREXTID, maintained in SM30 or with transaction EXTID_DN): one entry per person and identity. That table has done the job for years and it copes with a person who has several identities because each one is simply another row. For S/4HANA we did not want to carry the table over. We wanted the rule-based mapping of transaction CERTRULE instead. That is more than a like-for-like move because of the shape of our landscape:

  1. There are many BTP apps and most people use several of them.
  2. The same person can arrive with more than one e-mail address, depending on how they log on.
  3. Whichever app and whichever address it is, the ABAP system has to derive the one SAP user name of that person.

Keeping a table entry for every person, address and app is exactly what we want to leave behind. So I tested the mechanism with three questions:

  1. Can one rule in CERTRULE derive the SAP user for everybody whose e-mail address is in the user master?
  2. Can everything that does not fit the rule, such as a second address of the same person or an address that is not in the user master at all, be handled with an exception list of explicit mappings in the same transaction?
  3. Is the mapping independent of the app that makes the call?

Short answer: yes to all three. I ran two tests. In the first, two users logged on to a minimal BTP app with their e-mail address. The first was mapped by the rule and the second by an explicit mapping and the ABAP service reported two different SAP users. In the second, the same person logged on to two different BTP apps with two different e-mail addresses and both calls arrived in ABAP as the same SAP user. Getting there took three failures, each visible in a different log so the second half of this post is a troubleshooting map.

LANDSCAPE USED FOR THE TEST

What I used:

  • ABAP Platform Trial 2023 in Docker (system A4H, client 001). The image ships with a Cloud Connector 2.18.0 under /opt/sap/scc. It is not started with the system: /opt/sap/scc/daemon.sh start inside the container brings it up and the administration UI is then on port 8443.
  • SAP BTP trial (Cloud Foundry, US10) with a Cloud Identity Services subscription. The Identity Authentication tenant holds three test users on a domain of mine: planner@, technician@ and contractor@singhvikas.com.
  • For the first test, a minimal BTP app: only an approuter with one route to the ABAP system. No own code.
  • For the second test, a small CAP application with two Fiori elements apps, notifications and work orders, described further down.
  • Two ABAP users: JSMITH, created for this test without a password and the existing BWDEVELOPER.

The planner stands for the normal case: the address is also maintained in SU01, for JSMITH. The contractor stands for the exception: an address that no ABAP user carries. The technician comes in only in the second test, as a second address of the same person.

STEP 1. BTP SUBACCOUNT AND APP

1.1 Let the subaccount trust the identity provider

The user's e-mail address has to come from somewhere. In the subaccount, under Security → Trust Configuration, I chose Establish Trust and selected the Identity Authentication tenant. The new entry is shown as a custom identity provider for applications with origin key sap.custom, available for user logon.

Both identity providers stay active so the logon page of the app offers a choice. For the test, both users picked the Identity Authentication tenant.

1.2 Three service instances and an approuter

The app needs three service instances in the Cloud Foundry space: Authorization and Trust Management (plan application) for the logon, Destination (plan lite) to read the destination and Connectivity (plan lite) for the tunnel to the Cloud Connector.

The XSUAA instance was created with this descriptor. There are no scopes because being logged on is enough for this test.

{
  "xsappname": "certrule-whoami",
  "tenant-mode": "dedicated",
  "oauth2-configuration": {
    "redirect-uris": [ "https://*.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com/**" ]
  }
}

The app itself is two files. package.json pulls in the approuter:

{
  "name": "certrule-whoami-router",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "scripts": { "start": "node node_modules/@sap/approuter/approuter.js" },
  "dependencies": { "@sap/approuter": "^16.0.0" },
  "engines": { "node": ">=18" }
}

xs-app.json forwards /whoami to the ABAP service through the destination. The second route exposes the approuter's user API which is handy to see which attributes the token carries for the logged-on user.

{
  "welcomeFile": "/whoami",
  "authenticationMethod": "route",
  "routes": [
    {
      "source": "^/whoami$",
      "target": "/sap/bc/zpoc_whoami",
      "destination": "A4H_PP",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    },
    {
      "source": "^/user-api(.*)",
      "target": "$1",
      "service": "sap-approuter-userapi",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa"
    }
  ]
}

The manifest binds the three instances. I zipped the two files and deployed zip and manifest from the cockpit (Deploy Application in the space). cf push does the same.

applications:
  - name: certrule-whoami
    memory: 256M
    disk_quota: 512M
    buildpacks:
      - nodejs_buildpack
    random-route: true
    services:
      - whoami-xsuaa
      - whoami-destination
      - whoami-connectivity

1.3 The destination

Under Connectivity → Destinations I created A4H_PP: type HTTP, proxy type OnPremise, authentication PrincipalPropagation. The URL is the virtual host and port that the Cloud Connector will expose, written with http://. Encryption towards the ABAP system is configured in the Cloud Connector, not here.

STEP 2. ABAP SERVICE TO RETURN THE LOGGED ON USER

To see the result of the mapping I wanted the smallest possible service: an ICF handler that returns sy-uname.

CLASS zcl_poc_whoami DEFINITION PUBLIC FINAL CREATE PUBLIC.
  PUBLIC SECTION.
    INTERFACES if_http_extension.
ENDCLASS.

CLASS zcl_poc_whoami IMPLEMENTATION.
  METHOD if_http_extension~handle_request.
    server->response->set_content_type( 'application/json' ).
    server->response->set_cdata(
      |\{ "abapUser": "{ sy-uname }", "client": "{ sy-mandt }", | &&
      |"system": "{ sy-sysid }", "time": "{ sy-datum } { sy-uzeit }" \}| ).
    server->response->set_status( code = 200 reason = 'OK' ).
  ENDMETHOD.
ENDCLASS.

In SICF I created the node /default_host/sap/bc/zpoc_whoami, entered the class in the handler list and activated the service. No logon data is stored in the service so every caller has to authenticate.

STEP 3. CLOUD CONNECTOR

3.1 Connect it to the subaccount

In the BTP cockpit, Connectivity → Cloud Connectors offers Download Authentication Data. In the Cloud Connector I chose Add Subaccount and the option to configure it from that file. After that the cockpit shows one active connection.

3.2 Expose the ABAP service

Under Cloud to On-Premises → Access Control I added one system mapping and one resource:

SettingValue
Back-end typeABAP System
ProtocolHTTPS
Internal host and portvhcala4hci.dummy.nodomain:50001 (the HTTPS port of the ICM)
Virtual host and porta4h:443 (this is what the destination points to)
Principal typeX.509 Certificate
Host in request headerUse Virtual Host
Resource/sap/bc/zpoc_whoami, path and all sub-paths

The internal host name matters more than it looks. It has to match the name in the ABAP system's server certificate. More on that in the troubleshooting part.

3.3 Trust the identity providers of the subaccount

The Cloud Connector only issues a certificate for a user if it trusts whoever issued that user's token. On the Principal Propagation tab of Cloud to On-Premises, Synchronize reads the trust configuration of the subaccount. I got three entries: two for the subaccount's own token service and one for the Identity Authentication tenant.

3.4 System certificate, CA certificate and subject pattern

Under Configuration → On-Premises the Cloud Connector needs two certificates of its own and they do two different jobs:

  • The system certificate is the Cloud Connector's own identity. It presents it in the TLS handshake with the ABAP system. Mine is CN=SCC-A4H-SYSTEM,O=POC,C=AU.
  • The CA certificate signs the short-lived certificates that are created per user. Mine is CN=SCC-A4H-CA,O=POC,C=AU.

For this test I let the Cloud Connector create both as self-signed certificates. In a productive landscape both would come from your PKI.

The subject pattern decides what the per-user certificate looks like. I used CN=${email},O=POC,C=AU with a validity of 60 minutes. ${email} is filled from the user's token. The ICM trace later showed the real address in the subject so the attribute arrives correctly from the Identity Authentication tenant.

The same screen can create a sample certificate for a given e-mail address. Download one, CERTRULE needs it later as a template for the rule.

3.5 Trust the ABAP system's server certificate

The Cloud Connector is a TLS client towards the ABAP system and checks the server certificate. In the Backend Trust Store I added the certificate of the ICM's SSL server PSE to the allowlist. I exported it from STRUST (SSL server Standard, own certificate, Base64).

STEP 4. ABAP SYSTEM TRUST FOR THE CLOUD CONNECTOR

Three settings. None of them needed a restart.

4.1 STRUST: accept the system certificate

The Cloud Connector's system certificate goes into the certificate list of the SSL server Standard PSE. Import the file into the Certificate area, choose Add to Certificate List, save. The ICM picks up the changed PSE on its own and its trace notes IcmSSLPseChanged: SSL Certificate SAPSSLS.pse was changed.

4.2 Parameter icm/trusted_reverse_proxy to accept forwarded certificates

With 4.1 the Cloud Connector can log on to the ICM as itself. But the user's certificate does not arrive in the TLS handshake. It arrives in an HTTP header. The ICM only believes that header if the sender is listed as a trusted reverse proxy with subject and issuer of its certificate:

icm/trusted_reverse_proxy_0 = SUBJECT="CN=SCC-A4H-SYSTEM, O=POC, C=AU", ISSUER="CN=SCC-A4H-SYSTEM, O=POC, C=AU"

Copy subject and issuer exactly as STRUST shows them, including the blanks after the commas. RZ11 does not let you change this parameter and points to the ICM monitor instead.

The link in RZ11 (SMICM Parameter Changes) opens the ICM parameter list in change mode. I entered the value in the row icm/trusted_reverse_proxy [0] and chose Save Changes Locally. The ICM applies it immediately and warns that the change is not permanent and is deleted when the ICM is restarted so for anything lasting the same line belongs in the instance profile.

I did not touch icm/HTTPS/verify_client. The trace shows the ICM asking for a client certificate (auth_type=1 (ASK_CLIENT_CERT)) which is what the Cloud Connector needs.

4.3 Switch on rule-based mapping

login/certificate_mapping_rulebased = 1 activates the rules maintained in CERTRULE. The parameter is dynamic so RZ11 → Change Value is enough for a test. Like the previous one, it has to go into the profile to survive a restart.

STEP 5. CERTRULE RULE AND EXPLICIT MAPPING

5.1 The e-mail address in SU01

The rule will look for the ABAP user whose e-mail address equals the CN of the certificate. So the planner's address has to be in SU01, on the Address tab of JSMITH.

JSMITH has no password. On the Logon Data tab the password status is Password deactivated: SU01 lets you create a dialog user without one and such a user can only get in through single sign-on which is exactly what we want for people who arrive from BTP.

5.2 Create the rule from a sample certificate

CERTRULE works from an example. In change mode, import a sample certificate with the button next to the Subject field then choose Rule.

In the dialog I selected the CN as certificate attribute and E-Mail under Login As. The Subject Filter field lists the remaining attributes of the subject (O,C here) and I left it as proposed. The resulting rule has the subject filter CN=*,O=POC,C=AU and the issuer filter CN=SCC-A4H-CA,O=POC,C=AU: any certificate from this Cloud Connector CA with this organisation and country, whatever the CN.

The status area on the right only reflects what is saved. Directly after confirming the dialog it still said "Certificate not mapped". After Save it shows the result:

5.3 Rule result when no SAP user has the e-mail address

The same screen is a good simulator. I imported the contractor's sample certificate, an address that no ABAP user has. The rule matches but the user status is red: "Mapped email does not exist".

5.4 Explicit mapping for the second e-mail address

With the contractor's sample certificate loaded, choose Explicit Mapping and enter the ABAP user.

After saving, the entry appears on the Explicit Mappings tab and the status changes to "Certificate mapped explicitly".

SAP itself calls these entries exceptions. When I tried to add an explicit mapping for an address that the rule already maps to the same ABAP user, CERTRULE answered with the warning "You do not have to create an exception".

5.5 Two e-mail addresses mapped to one SAP user

This is the case we have: one person, two addresses, one SAP user. I simulated it with a certificate for another address (an invented example.com one) and mapped it explicitly to JSMITH, the user that the rule already finds through the planner's address.

CERTRULE accepts it and reports the same SAP user. So the primary address needs no entry at all because the rule covers it and every additional address of that person is one line in the exception list. Here I only checked it with a sample certificate and removed the entry again. The second test further down does it with a real logon.

5.6 Order of rule and explicit mapping

In everything I saw, the explicit mapping came first:

  • The contractor's certificate also matches rule 0. The status nevertheless reports the explicit mapping and the real logon ended up as BWDEVELOPER.
  • For a short test I also gave an address that the rule maps an explicit mapping to the same user. The status switched from "mapped with rule 0" to "mapped explicitly".

FIRST TEST WITH TWO USERS AND TWO SAP USERS

Each user opened the app URL in a fresh private browser window (the planner in Chrome, the contractor in Edge), chose the Identity Authentication tenant on the logon page and signed in with e-mail address and password. No ABAP password was involved. JSMITH does not even have one.

Logged on to the BTP app asSubject of the certificate created by the Cloud ConnectorHow CERTRULE mapped itABAP user
planner@singhvikas.comCN=planner@singhvikas.com, O=POC, C=AURule 0: CN → e-mail address in SU01JSMITH
contractor@singhvikas.comCN=contractor@singhvikas.com, O=POC, C=AUExplicit mappingBWDEVELOPER

SECOND TEST WITH TWO APPS AND ONE SAP USER

The first test answered the questions with two users who end up as two SAP users. The case we actually have is the other way round: one person, two addresses, several apps and one SAP user at the end. So I built a second, slightly more realistic application and ran it with two identities that both have to arrive in ABAP as JSMITH.

The application

It is a small SAP CAP application (Node.js) that simulates plant maintenance: notifications and work orders with equipment, operations and status codes and sample data from CSV files in an in-memory SQLite database. It has two services and two Fiori elements apps, both list report and object page, built from annotations only:

  • App 1, Notifications, for the planner. Report a problem against a piece of equipment and create a work order from it. Service PlannerService, requires the role Planner.
  • App 2, Work orders, for the technician. Release and complete orders. Service TechnicianService, requires the role Technician.

The approuter guards the two apps and their OData services with two scopes and xs-security.json turns them into the role collections PM_Planner and PM_Technician:

{ "source": "^/odata/v4/planner/(.*)$",    "destination": "srv-api", "scope": "$XSAPPNAME.Planner" },
{ "source": "^/odata/v4/technician/(.*)$", "destination": "srv-api", "scope": "$XSAPPNAME.Technician" }

The only custom UI code is a strip at the bottom of each app. It calls a function whoami() in the CAP service and the service forwards the call to /sap/bc/zpoc_whoami from Step 2 through the same destination A4H_PP as before, this time from CAP instead of from an approuter route:

// package.json: "A4H": { "kind": "rest", "credentials": { "destination": "A4H_PP", "path": "/sap/bc" } }
srv.on('whoami', async req => {
  const a4h = await cds.connect.to('A4H');
  const r = await a4h.send({ method: 'GET', path: '/zpoc_whoami' });
  return { iasUser: req.user.id, abapUser: r.abapUser, abapClient: r.client, abapSystem: r.system };
});

The destination, the Cloud Connector and the ABAP side are exactly as described in Steps 1 to 5. Nothing was added there for the second app and that is the point: the application does not know JSMITH and the ABAP system does not know the application.

The two identities

The planner is the same Identity Authentication user as in the first test and the technician is the second one, technician@singhvikas.com. Each of them got one role collection in the subaccount. The domain has no mailbox behind it so the users were created with a password set by the administrator and the flag "Verify Email" ticked. Without it the logon stops at "Verify Your Email".

On the ABAP side nothing changes for the planner: the address is on JSMITH in SU01 (5.1) so rule 0 maps it. The technician's address is in no user master. With a sample certificate for it, CERTRULE shows the rule matching and the red user status "Mapped email does not exist", exactly as in 5.3:

One explicit mapping to JSMITH later, the status is "Certificate mapped explicitly" and the E-mail field on the right shows the planner's address: the address CERTRULE knows for JSMITH from the user master. This is 5.5 again, now with a real logon behind it.

The sample certificate was generated with openssl with the same subject and issuer as the Cloud Connector produces. CERTRULE works with the subject and issuer names only so the sample does not have to be signed by the real CA. The Cloud Connector's own "create sample certificate" function gives the same result.

The result

Both apps opened in fresh private windows, the planner in Chrome, the technician in Edge. Each logged on with their own address and each strip shows the ABAP user the call ran as:

AppLogged on to BTP asHow CERTRULE mapped itABAP user
App 1, Notificationsplanner@singhvikas.comRule 0: CN → e-mail address in SU01JSMITH
App 2, Work orderstechnician@singhvikas.comExplicit mappingJSMITH

Two apps, two logons, one SAP user and the only thing that changed in ABAP for the second address was one line in the exception list.

IMPACT FOR MULTIPLE APPS AND MULTIPLE E-MAIL ADDRESSES PER USER

  • The app does not appear in the mapping. The ABAP system only sees the certificate that the Cloud Connector created. The ICM trace further down shows it: a subject with the e-mail address, an issuer, nothing about the calling app. Every app that goes through the same Cloud Connector with the same subject pattern therefore hits the same rule and the same exceptions. The second test ran two apps, one of them from CAP rather than from an approuter route and nothing about them appears in CERTRULE.
  • The rule removes the per-user entries. Whoever has the address from the identity provider in SU01 needs no mapping entry.
  • The exception list holds only what is left: additional addresses of a person and people whose address is not in the user master. The amount of maintenance is the number of exceptions, not users times apps.
  • Which address arrives is decided before ABAP. It is the e-mail attribute in the token of the identity provider the app trusts. Each identity provider has to be trusted by the Cloud Connector as well. Synchronize showed one entry per provider.
  • One subject pattern was enough here. The Cloud Connector lets you define several subject pattern rules with conditions. I did not use that.

TROUBLESHOOTING THE THREE ERRORS

The call passes through four components and each of them fails in its own way. What helped most was reading the symptom in the browser first because it tells you how far the request got.

What the browser showsHow far the request gotWhere to look
Plain text "Invalid server certificate"Reached the Cloud Connector which refused to talk to the ABAP systemCloud Connector: Log And Trace Files
A user/password popup (HTTP 401 with Basic authentication)Reached the ABAP system. TLS and the Cloud Connector are fine but the certificate logon did not happenICM trace then HTTP log then work process trace
The JSON but with the wrong ABAP userEverything technical worksCERTRULE with a sample certificate

Error 1 Invalid server certificate

The first call returned this one line. It comes from the Cloud Connector, not from the app and not from ABAP. Its trace file scc_core.trc had the same text and the target of the failed connection:

#WARN#...OutboundConnectionErrorHandler#tunnel-client-10-1#...#Protocol processing error:
   ...HttpProtocolException: Invalid server certificate
#ERROR#...#Write operation FAILED ... [... R:vhcala4hci/172.17.0.2:50001].
   Cause: io.netty.handler.ssl.SslClosedEngineException: SSLEngine closed already

The message does not say what is invalid. In my case the certificate was in the trust store already. The problem was the host name. The server certificate of the trial system is issued to *.dummy.nodomain and my system mapping used the short name vhcala4hci as internal host. After changing the internal host to vhcala4hci.dummy.nodomain, the availability check in the Access Control list turned to Reachable and the error was gone. SAP describes the same cause for the same message in KBA 3084008.

The ICM trace at its default level showed nothing for these attempts so do not wait for the ABAP side to explain this one.

Error 2 Password popup instead of the result

The next call produced a logon popup in the browser.

This is progress: the request is in the ABAP system. I worked through it from the outside in.

ICM trace. In SMICM, Goto → Trace Level → Increase sets level 2. Repeat the call then use Trace Search for certificate. A healthy hand-over from the Cloud Connector looks like this (thread numbers removed):

HttpHandleCertificate: Client certificate received: with len=1264,
   subj="CN=SCC-A4H-SYSTEM, O=POC, C=AU", issuer="CN=SCC-A4H-SYSTEM, O=POC, C=AU"
HttpCertIsReverseProxyTrustworthy: intermediate is trustworthy (i:s):
HttpIsReverseProxyTrustworthy: intermediary is trusted
Forwarded Client certificate: subject="CN=<e-mail address>, O=POC, C=AU",
   issuer="CN=SCC-A4H-CA, O=POC, C=AU"
HTTP request [...] Accept trusted forwarded certificate (received via HTTPS with
   trusted certificate): subject="CN=<e-mail address>, O=POC, C=AU", ...
HttpModSerializeCertificate: client cert copied to MPI

These lines answer three questions at once: the system certificate was accepted (4.1), the reverse proxy is trusted (4.2) and the subject pattern produced what you expect (3.4). If the trusted_reverse_proxy value is wrong, SAP KBA 3017609 lists what appears here instead: "no trust relationship to intermediary specified", "intermediary is NOT trusted" and "Reject untrusted forwarded certificate". I did not get those, my ICM side was fine. Goto → Trace Level → Default sets the level back afterwards.

HTTP log. The ICM's access log is in the instance's log directory (AL11, DIR_LOGGING, file http-<date>.log). Each of my failed calls is one line with status 401 and a dash where the client and user normally stand. Successful requests show something like 001/JSMITH there. It confirms that the request ended without a user and gives exact times to search for in the other traces.

Security audit log. SM20 had no entry for these failed logons in my system as delivered. I would not rely on it for this problem without checking its configuration first.

Work process trace. In SM50, select the dialog work processes and choose Administration → Trace → Active Components: level 2 and component Security. Repeat the call then Administration → Trace → Save Files to get the dev_w* files as text. Two lines mattered:

M  ThPlgISetSslCertificate: show client certificate
M  ICTSYS: GetCookie, options=0, path='' name/value= 'sap-ssolist....'
M  ICTSYS: BASE64Unescape 'O2M9dmhjYWxhNGhjaV9BNEhfMDBfMDAx' -> 0 ';c=vhcala4hci_A4H_00_001'
...
M  ICTSYS: SetStatus 401 Unauthorized
M  ICTSYS: AddHeaderField 'WWW-Authenticate....'

The first line says the user certificate did reach the work process. The cookie is the reason it was not used. As far as I can tell from the traces and from the logon handler (class CL_HTTP_SERVER_NET), a failed certificate logon leaves a cookie sap-ssolist that contains ;c= plus instance name and client. On the next request the handler reads that cookie as "this client's certificate was already rejected here" and skips the certificate logon altogether. The approuter passes the cookie on to the browser, the browser sends it back every time and so every retry from the same browser session fails, even after the original cause is gone.

That is what happened to me. I kept reloading the same tab and kept changing settings that were not the problem. The moment the users logged on from a fresh private window, both calls worked. Restore the default trace components in SM50 when you are done, level 2 fills the trace files quickly.

What made the very first attempt fail, I cannot say for certain. The likely cause is time: SM50 showed a work process clock roughly 25 minutes behind real time around that attempt (the work process traces from the same period also contain timestamp-check errors) and a certificate that was issued a few minutes ago is "not yet valid" for a system that lives in the past. A Docker system on a laptop that has been asleep is prone to this. The clock was back in step later and I did not reproduce the failure.

While searching, I also changed the logon procedure of the ICF service from Standard to an alternative list with "Use all logon procedures" ticked. The calls started working only with the fresh browser session so I believe the standard procedure would have been enough. I left the changed setting in place and did not go back to prove it.

Error 3 Wrong user or no user

This is the cheapest one to check and it needs no end-to-end call. Create a sample certificate in the Cloud Connector for the e-mail address in question, import it in CERTRULE and read the status: mapped by rule, mapped explicitly or "Mapped email does not exist". If the address in the sample is not what you expected, call /user-api/currentUser on the approuter to see what the token really contains.

LESSONS LEARNT

  • The Subject Filter field in the Create Rule dialog is not a free-text filter. It holds the list of remaining attributes. When I typed CN=* into it, CERTRULE refused with "Use the input help to specify valid data" and I wrongly concluded that a subject with only a CN cannot be used. It can: with the field left as proposed, a sample certificate CN=<e-mail> gave the rule CN=* and mapped correctly. Adding O and C to the subject pattern is still a good idea because it makes the rule narrower.
  • CERTRULE status is "based on persistence". Save before you judge whether a new rule or mapping works.
  • The internal host in the Cloud Connector must match the server certificate. "Invalid server certificate" does not mention host names.
  • One failed certificate logon poisons the browser session. Test again in a new private window, not with the reload button.
  • Dynamic parameters are easy to lose. login/certificate_mapping_rulebased and icm/trusted_reverse_proxy_0 were both set dynamically here. After a restart the app would show the password popup again.
  • A test user whose address cannot receive mail gets stuck at "Verify Your Email" in Identity Authentication. Set the password as administrator and tick Verify Email on the user.

SUMMARY

One rule in CERTRULE does the job the per-user entries in USREXTID did for us in ECC. Everybody whose e-mail address is maintained in SU01 is mapped by it and no entry is needed for them.

Everything that does not fit the rule goes into the exception list in the same transaction: a second address of the same person or an address that is not in the user master. The maintenance effort is the number of exceptions, not users times apps.

The app does not appear in the mapping. The ABAP system only sees the certificate the Cloud Connector creates so every app that goes through the same Cloud Connector hits the same rule and the same exceptions. The second test showed it with a real logon: two apps, two addresses, one SAP user.

Most of the time went into three failures and each one shows up in a different log. The one that cost the most was the browser session: after a failed certificate logon, test again in a fresh private window, not with the reload button.

REFERENCES

Source code of the second test's application (CAP, two Fiori elements apps, approuter, MTA): github.com/viksingh/pm-demo-certrule

SAP KBA 3084008: "Invalid server certificate" in the Cloud Connector when the internal host does not match the certificate

SAP KBA 3017609: principal propagation fails, "intermediary is NOT trusted" in dev_icm

SAP Learning: Setting Up SAP S/4HANA for Principal Propagation

Setting up Principal Propagation (SAP blog)

SAP Help Portal, Cloud Connector: "Configuring Principal Propagation"

SAP Help Portal, ABAP Platform: "Rule-Based Certificate Mapping" (transaction CERTRULE)

entry.title: Agentic AI on BTP: Connecting Agents to SAP OData APIs without an MCP Server
entry.content:
Introduction

Every agent in my app reaches its tools through MCP servers or built-in connectors. For SAP development that works great, an MCP server like ARC-1 gives the agent everything it needs on the ABAP side. Business data is a different story. When an agent needs to know which purchase requisitions are waiting or what is planned for next week, it needs the SAP APIs themselves.

This is the fifth post in the series. The previous one turned a specialist into a deep agent: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/agentic-ai-on-btp-turning-a-specialist-into-a-deep-agent/ba-p/14501349

In this blog post, I’ll show you how agents in the app now call SAP OData services directly and why I did not put an MCP server in between this time.

Problem

The obvious way to give an agent access to an OData service is an MCP server that wraps it. I did that before, I even built an OData to MCP proxy. For this app it meant:

  • One more app to run. Build it, deploy it, secure it and keep it running next to the agent app, for every system you want to reach.
  • One more hop for the user. The agent app already has the user’s JWT. With an MCP server in between, that identity has to be forwarded once more before it reaches the destination and the Cloud Connector.
  • The model sees everything. A generic wrapper exposes the full service: every entity set, every field. Whatever the SAP user can read, the model can read.
  • Too many tools. One tool per entity set or operation fills the context before the agent has done anything. Same problem as in post 3.
  • Writes without control. Who decides which agent may create or change data in SAP and where do you see what it did?

Solution

The app now has OData services as a built-in toolset (builtin:odata), next to Gmail, Outlook, SharePoint and the others. It runs in-process, so there is no extra server.

An admin curates a catalogue in the admin UI: which services exist for agents, which entity sets, which fields and which operations:

A service is imported from its $metadata. Each service has its own identity: the BTP destination and who it runs as, the signed-in user or a technical user. The purpose and “not for” lines are what the agent reads to decide when to use it:

Nothing arrives enabled. Per entity set you tick list, get, create, update and delete and per field whether the agent may read it, filter on it or write it. Personal data is marked by hand, so you see what you are giving away:

On the agent, you add the toolset “OData services”, pick the catalogue services and decide whether it may write:

The agent gets exactly two tools, whatever the number of services: search_operations to find what it can read or do and execute_operation to run one of those by name. It never gets a URL, a destination name or a free path. A name the catalogue doesn’t hold doesn’t exist for the model.

No custom code per service. Just configuration. 🙂

Why direct OData and not MCP

MCP is the right choice when the same API needs to serve several AI clients, Joule, Copilot, Claude and so on. That’s exactly why I built the proxy. But here the only consumer is the agent inside this app and then the extra layer adds a server, a hop and a protocol without adding anything else.

Going direct also lets me enforce rules in code instead of in the prompt:

  • Only readable fields reach the model. Whatever SAP sends back, the response is cut to the fields marked readable in the catalogue. $select is always sent and a filter can only use allowed fields, so it can’t probe hidden values.
  • Identity per service, not per agent. The admin decides who SAP sees: the user through principal propagation or a technical user. OnPremise systems go through the connectivity service and the Cloud Connector, like any other BTP app.
  • Writes need two switches. The operation has to be enabled in the catalogue AND the agent needs “Allow writes”. Function imports and actions count as writes too, unless they are marked as only reading. In SAP, release and approve are function imports after all.
  • No audit row, no write. Every write gets an intent row in the audit log before anything is sent and a result row afterwards. If the audit can’t be written, nothing goes to SAP.
  • The model never holds an ETag. It gets an opaque handle, the real ETag stays on the server and goes out as If-Match.

What about the SAP API Policy?

SAP’s API Policy (April 2026) says agents may only call SAP APIs through an endorsed SAP architecture. These agents run on SAP BTP, inside SAP’s own platform, not as a third-party tool reaching in from outside. SAP’s Architecture Center describes this setup: pro-code agents in your own BTP subaccount, with Pydantic AI as one of the frameworks and A2A to Joule. Interfaces in the customer namespace, like the Z service in my example, remain permitted.

I’m not a lawyer, so check your own scenario against SAP’s information:

  • SAP API Policy overview: https://assets.dm.ux.sap.com/sap-user-groups/pdfs/260530_sap_api_policy_overview.pdf
  • Agentic AI & AI Agents on SAP Business AI Platform: https://architecture.learning.sap.com/docs/ref-arch/98efa0

What it looks like in a run

The example in the screenshots is a planning check. The planning lives in an Excel workbook on SharePoint, SAP holds what is actually registered. Nobody compares the two until someone notices a gap.

The agent reads the planning from SharePoint, searches the catalogue once and then reads the registrations in SAP week by week, nine calls side by side. The differences go out by mail:

Note the two catalogue entries on the list page. They point to the same SAP service, once as a technical user for this scheduled check and once as the signed-in user for an agent that is called from another app. Same API, two identities, decided by the admin and not by the agent.

Conclusion

For SAP development I keep using MCP servers, they serve more than this app. For business data that only this app’s agents need, a curated OData catalogue does the same job with less: no extra server, the user’s identity straight to SAP and the rules in code where the model can’t talk its way around them.

The added value is mostly in the control. An admin decides per service what agents can see and per agent what they can change, without a redeploy and with a record of every write.

Contributions and feedback are welcome, the full source code is on GitHub: https://github.com/lemaiwo/btp-dynamic-multiagent-app

Links

  • Post 4, deep agents: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/agentic-ai-on-btp-turning-a-specialist-into-a-deep-agent/ba-p/14501349
  • Post 3, workflows: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/agentic-ai-on-btp-chaining-agents-into-a-workflow/ba-p/14496861
  • Post 2, scheduled runs: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/agentic-ai-on-btp-running-your-agents-unattended-on-a-schedule/ba-p/14493817
  • Post 1, configuring agents: https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/agentic-ai-on-btp-configuring-code-based-agents-on-the-fly/ba-p/14488352
  • Source code: https://github.com/lemaiwo/btp-dynamic-multiagent-app
