entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 2: Content Agent and destinations in Dev
entry.content:
Part 2 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 1 we built CTMS in Central: a service key, a source node, a target node and the route. In this part we move to the Dev subaccount and set up the packer, Content Agent, plus the three connections Integration Suite needs to start a transport.

 

Before you start

In Dev, SAP Integration Suite must be subscribed and the Cloud Integration capability activated. Step 1 fails without it (see "What tripped me up" below).

Step 1: Process Integration Runtime instance and key

This instance lets Content Agent read your integration packages.

  • Create a service instance of SAP Process Integration Runtime with plan api.
  • Give it the roles WorkspacePackagesRead, WorkspacePackagesEdit and WorkspacePackagesTransport, with grant type client credentials.
  • Create a service key. You need its url, clientid, clientsecret and tokenurl.

Step 2: Content Agent instance and key

  • Create a service instance of Content Agent service with plan standard. This is the packer.
  • Create a service key. You need its uri and, from the uaa section, clientid, clientsecret and url.

Step 3: The three destinations

Go to Connectivity > Destinations in Dev and create three destinations. All three use type HTTP, proxy type Internet and authentication OAuth2ClientCredentials. Type the names exactly as below: Integration Suite looks them up by name.

NameURLClient ID / secretToken Service URL
ContentAssemblyServiceuri from the Content Agent keyuaa clientid / clientsecretuaa url + /oauth/token
CloudIntegrationurl from the Process Integration Runtime key + /api/1.0/transportmodule/Transportclientid / clientsecrettokenurl
TransportManagementServiceuri from the CTMS key (Part 1)uaa clientid / clientsecretuaa url + /oauth/token

TransportManagementService needs one more thing. Under Additional Properties, add sourceSystemId with the exact name of the source node from Part 1. This tells CTMS which node the parcel is dropped at.

 

Left: the sourceSystemId property (value blurred). Right: Check Connection on the same destination. Read the message carefully, see below.

What tripped me up in my setup

  • The runtime instance would not create. My first Process Integration Runtime instance in Dev ended in "Creation Failed" with this service broker message: "Service instance could not be created for Process Integration Runtime because the required service/capability is not active for this subaccount. Please subscribe to SAP Integration Suite, and once you've done that, activate required SAP Integration Suite capability, such as Cloud Integration or Graph. Then, try again." The instance is only a door to a running Cloud Integration, so that capability has to exist first. Once it was active, I created the instance again from the Service Marketplace and it went through.
  • A green Check Connection proves less than it seems. The message says "HTTP request (without authentication) ... succeeded". It only shows the address is reachable. It does not test the client ID or secret. My client ID mismatch in TransportManagementService did not show up here; it showed up when I opened the Content Agent screen, and that screen worked as soon as I fixed the client ID.
  • Leave the extra options alone. I kept "Use mTLS for token retrieval" and "Use Basic credentials for token service" unticked and Token Service URL Type on Dedicated. For BTP services talking to each other with service keys, the defaults are right. Change them only if your security team requires certificates instead of client secrets.

Roles for this part

Only the instance roles from step 1. They belong to the Process Integration Runtime instance, not to any user. The user roles you need to click Transport come in Part 4, and Part 7 lists them all.

What comes next

Dev can now pack a parcel and drop it at the source node. In Part 3 we go back to Central and set up the second Content Agent, the one that unpacks the parcel into the target, and finally fill in the target node's destination.

entry.title: MCP and SAP Integration from concept to practice. Part 2
entry.content:
Introduction :

Imagine a customer service agent typing : 

"Please give me all updates of order no 1103"  and getting back, in seconds: "Order 1103 for XYZ Technologies is Delayed because of a supplier shortage. New delivery date: 12 Oct 2026." No transaction codes, no reports, no searching.

In Part 1 I explained the idea: MCP gives AI agents a standard way to discover and call enterprise capabilities, and SAP Integration Suite stays the layer that keeps this secure and governed. I ended with one question : MCP can open the door for AI agents, but who gets the keys?

Now it’s time to move from theory to practice, and build the lock.

In this post I answer it with a working example. I build an MCP server on SAP BTP Cloud Foundry, put SAP API Management in front of it, and ask it questions from Cline , an AI Agent in VS Code. Everything runs on a free BTP trial.

What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)? 

MCP is an open standard that lets AI assistants call tools in your systems instead of guessing from their training data. A tool is simply a function with a name, a description and an input schema, for example get_order_updates(orderId) .

The interesting part:  The AI decides which tool to call by reading its description. We never write "if the user says order, call this API". We describe the tool well, and the agent figures out the rest.

Think of it this way:  An API is built for developers; an MCP tool is built for AI agents.

Architecture Overview 

How it works:

1. You ask Cline a question in plain language.
2. Cline reads the tool list from the MCP server and picks the right tool.
3. The request goes to SAP API Management with an API key and an XSUAA token.
4. API Management checks the key, validates the JWT and counts the call against a quota.
5. The MCP server runs the tool, and Cline turns the result into a plain-language answer.

Prerequisites  

  1. SAP BTP Trial Account with the Cloud Foundry environment and a space (mcp-demo) .
  2. SAP Integration Suite with APIM capability activated, including the Developer Hub.
  3. Node.js version 20 or higher.
  4. Cloud Foundry CLI (cf) installed.
  5. VS Code with Cline extension. Cline’s free model is enough; my test runs cost $0.00.

Link : Source code , scripts and full setup commands : GitHub repository: sap-mcp-server (user: himaniarya159-dev).

The Scenario: Customers and Sales Orders

The MCP server knows five customers and their sales orders. Each order has items, an amount and a dated history (created, confirmed, shipped, delayed…). It's sample data on purpose: The goal is to show the pattern. Real SAP S/4HANA data is the topic of Part 3.

Each tool is registered with a name, a description and a Zod input schema. That description is all the agent needs  GitHub repository: sap-mcp-server (user: himaniarya159-dev).

Security Considerations 

A deployed MCP server without protection means any agent that knows the URL can call every tool. Here is how this setup closes that door. 

  1. Two identities, checked at the gateway : 
  • VerifyAPIKey : Checks which application is calling, using the key from the Developer Hub. Fails with 401 FailedToResolveAPIKey.
  • VerifyJWT : Checks for a valid, time-limited XSUAA token (RS256 signature and issuer). Fails with 401.
  • Quota : Allows at most 10 calls per minute per application. Fails with 500 QuotaViolation. 

All three sit in the proxy's PreFlow. The MCP server itself stays simple: it only implements tools.

       2. Which value goes where : The XSUAA service key contains three kinds of values, and each belongs in a different place:

Don't make a mistake to pasting an access token into the VerifyJWT policy. The policy needs the public key that verifies tokens, not a token. ( Explained in Development part )

        3. No hardcoded credentials :

The API key and XSUAA credentials live only in a local .env file that is never committed. A small helper, get-token.js , turns them into a Bearer token for Cline.

       4. Grounded answers :

A rules file, .clinerules/sap-assistant.md , tells Cline to answer only from the MCP tools, never from the project files, and never to invent data. Ask for order 9999 and you get "not found", not a made-up order.

Step-by-Step Deployment :

Step 1: Run the MCP server locally 

git clone https://< your git cred >//.git
cd sap-mcp-server
npm install
npm start

Get the code from GitHub repository: sap-mcp-server (user: himaniarya159-dev) and start it:

The server is now running on your PC. It has two addresses: /mcp ,where AI agents talk to it, and /health , which tells Cloud Foundry the app is alive. The last line lists the four tools the agent will be able to use.

Step 2 : Deploy to Cloud Foundry

Set your own unique route in

 manifest.yml

, then:

Run 

cf push

 

Check https://<your-app-route>/health , which returns

 {"status":"UP"}

.

Step 3 : Create the API proxy 

Integration Suite→ Configure → APIs → Create:

Save → Deploy. No resources are needed: MCP uses a single POST endpoint.

Step 4 : Add the policies

Open the proxy →Policies  → ProxyEndPoint→ PreFlow and add the three policies in this order. Every request must pass all three before it reaches the MCP server.

  • VerifyAPIKey: Which application is calling? : The client sends a key in the X-API-Key header. API Management checks that it belongs to a registered application. ( Explained in Step 5.) 
  •                          
  • VerifyJWT:  is the token valid? : The client also sends an XSUAA access token ( Authorization Bearer ). The policy checks its signature with XSUAA’s public key and checks who issued it. A token expires after a few hours, so a leaked token is far less risky than a leaked key. First create XSUAA and a service key: 

          Run : 

cf create-service xsuaa application mcp-xsuaa

         or We can also do it with SAP BTP trial Authorization and Trust Management service in service marketplace subscribe it and then create a service key for it .

  • Quota: How many calls are allowed? : Each application may make 10 calls per minute. This protects the backend from an agent stuck in a loop. It comes last, so only checked and trusted calls count against the limit.

 

 

Step 5 : Get an API key :

Engage → Products: create a product with SAP-MCP-API and Publish it. Then in the Developer Hub , create an application for the product. Its Key is your API key. 

Step 6 : Prove the policies work

(Two surprises from my test run )

  • “Too many calls” arrives as a server error : The web’s standard answer to “slow down” is 429 Too Many Requests. SAP API Management’s Quota policy answers with 500 and policies.ratelimit.QuotaViolation instead. Why it matters: a client, or an AI agent, that sees a 500 thinks the server crashed and may simply retry, which makes the traffic worse. Always check the error text, not just the number. If your clients expect 429, you can map it in the proxy’s fault rules.
  • The limit was 10, but 12 calls got through : With Distributed set to true, several gateway nodes share one counter. Picture two ticket booths at a concert selling from one shared stock: each booth sells on its own and they compare numbers every few seconds. In a fast burst, both sell a few extra tickets before they sync. That’s what happened in my test. The quota is a reliable safety net for sustained traffic, not a perfect counter for a split-second burst.

Connecting Cline 

Step 1: Connect to the local server : 

Install the Cline extension in VS Code, then go to wrench icon → MCP → Edit Configuration 

The server turns green and lists the four tools.( here two MCP server are configured local and APIM ) 

Step 2: Ask your first question : 

In the Cline chat, type ("Please give me all updates of order no 1103") for local server testing ( sap-mcp-local) should be green and for SAP API Management testing ( sap-mcp-apim) should be green . Cline picks get_order_updates on its own, calls it, and answers:

Step 3: Switch to SAP API Management :

Now the real test: The same question, but through the secured gateway. Disable the local server and add the proxy with both headers:  In Cline We add a second MCP server entry that points to the API Proxy URL instead of localhost , and gives it the two “keys” from the Security section:

  • X-API-Key : The application key from the Developer Hub.
  • Authorization : Bearer plus a fresh XSUAA token. The repo’s get-token.js creates it for us. 

The ready-to-copy configuration is in theGitHub repository: sap-mcp-server (user: himaniarya159-dev) README.md .

Stop the local server, so an answer can only come through API Management, and ask again: ( “Please give me all updates of order no 1101”) .

Same question style, same kind of answer, but now every tool call has passed the API key, JWT and quota checks.

We also can try these too 

Wrapping Up: MCP Meets the Gateway 

We started with one question from Part 1, who gets the keys?, and ended with a concrete answer: SAP API Management does. The MCP server only focuses on tools, the gateway decides who may call them and how often, and the AI agent turns the results into answers a business user understands.

Key Takeaways :

  • The description is the interface. The agent chose every tool from its name and description alone.
  • MCP doesn't replace SAP Integration Suite. API Management added the security, quotas and tracing without a single change to the MCP server.
  • New tools are protected automatically. The proxy forwards all MCP traffic to one endpoint, so every new tool sits behind the same policies.
  • Grounding matters. A simple rules file keeps the agent to real data: "not found" instead of a confident guess.
  • It's reusable. Swap the sample data for an SAP API and the whole chain stays the same.

What's Next : 

In Part 3, the same MCP server reads customers and sales orders live from SAP S/4HANA through a BTP destination. Cline, API Management, the tools and the questions stay the same; only the data source changes.

Related Resources : 

  • GitHub repository:  sap-mcp-server (user: himaniarya159-dev)
  • Part 1: MCP and SAP Integration: Connecting AI Agents with Enterprise APIs
  • Model Context Protocol
  • SAP API Management on SAP Help Portal: https://help.sap.com/docs/sap-api-management
  • Cline

Himani Arya

SAP Integration Developer

entry.title: Stop Clicking, Start Scripting: Automate BTP Role Collection Mapping to IAS Groups via REST APIs
entry.content:
Introduction

Picture this: a customer is going live with a new SAP BTP landscape. Their IAS tenant already has user groups set up, their role collections are defined, and all that's left is connecting the two. Simple enough: in the BTP cockpit, navigate to Security → Trust Configuration → your IAS trust → Role Collection Mappings, and add one mapping at a time.

Now imagine doing that hundreds of times.

That was the reality for one of my customers. 130 role collections, each needing to be mapped to its corresponding IAS user group. At a conservative 3-4 minutes per mapping, finding the right collection, typing the group name exactly right, saving, repeat. You're looking at close to 8 hours of repetitive, error-prone cockpit work.

As a BTP consultant, I've seen this scenario play out more than once. And every time, the frustration is the same: the platform has everything you need, yet you're stuck doing something a machine should be doing for you.

In this blog post, you will learn how to use the SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service REST API to map BTP role collections to IAS user groups programmatically, saving hours of manual work, eliminating typo-induced errors, and giving you a reusable script you can run across every environment in your landscape.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure you have the following in place:

  • Subaccount Administrator role collection assigned to your user in the target BTP subaccount
  • A BTP subaccount with an IAS tenant configured as a custom identity provider
  • IAS user groups already created and populated with users
  • BTP CLI installed and configured
  • A REST client for testing: curl, Postman, or Bruno all work fine
  • Node.js (v18+) for the automation script (if you're creating a Node.js script like me)

 

Let's get scripting

Step 1 — Get API Credentials via the BTP CLI

To call the XSUAA REST API, you need a client credential pair. The cleanest way to get one is directly through the BTP CLI. No service instance or service key required.

btp login --sso
btp target --subaccount <SUBACCOUNT_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

Note:  This is the current recommended approach, replacing the deprecated apiaccess XSUAA service plan. If you come across older tutorials using "cf create-service xsuaa apiaccess" that approach still works but is being phased out.

The command returns a JSON object. Save these four values, you'll need all of them:

  • clientid
  • clientsecret
  • url (the token endpoint)
  • apiurl (the API base URL)

Step 2 — Get a Bearer Token

With the credentials in hand, request an OAuth token using the client credentials flow:

curl --request POST \
--url <url> \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
--data 'client_id=<clientid>' \
--data 'client_secret=<clientsecret>' \
--data 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
--data 'response_type=token'

Copy the access_token value from the response. You'll use it as a Bearer token in the next steps.

Step 3 — Check Existing Mappings (Optional but Recommended)

Before writing anything, it's worth checking what mappings already exist for your IAS identity provider. This gives you a baseline and avoids surprises:

curl --request GET \
--url <apiurl>/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/<IAS_ORIGIN_KEY>/attributes \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'authorization: Bearer <access_token>'

Where to find the IAS Origin Key: In your BTP subaccount, go to Security → Trust Configuration and click on your IAS trust entry. The Origin Key is shown in the detail panel. It typically looks like <something>.accounts.ondemand.com.

Step 4 — Create a Single Mapping

Now for the actual mapping call. Let's do one manually first to confirm everything works before running a bulk script:

curl --request POST \
--url <apiurl>/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/<IAS_ORIGIN_KEY>/attributes \
--header 'accept: application/json' \
--header 'authorization: Bearer <access_token>' \
--header 'content-type: application/json' \
--data '{
"attributeName": "Groups",
"attributeValue": "<IAS_Group_Name>",
"operator": "equals",
"roleCollectionName": "<BTP_Role_Collection_Name>"
}'

A few things to pay attention to:

  • attributeName must be exactly "Groups" with capital G, case-sensitive. This is the single most common mistake, and it fails without a helpful error message, so double-check this first.
  • attributeValue is the IAS group name, not the group ID.
  • roleCollectionName must match the role collection name exactly as it appears in the BTP cockpit.

A successful call returns HTTP 201 with the created mapping. To verify: go to BTP Cockpit → Security → Role Collections → open your role collection → User Groups tab. Your IAS group should now appear there.

Step 5 — Scale It Up: Automate with a Node.js Script

One mapping confirmed, now let's do all 130. The script below reads a list of mappings from a JSON file, fetches a token, and loops through each entry.

Project structure:

  • mappings.json – your list of group → role collection pairs
  • map-roles.mjs – the script
  • .env – credentials (never commit or publish this!)

.env

TOKEN_URL=https://<subdomain>.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token
CLIENT_ID=<your-client-id>
CLIENT_SECRET=<your-client-secret>
API_URL=https://api.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com
IAS_ORIGIN_KEY=<your-ias-origin-key>

mappings.json

[
    {
        "iasGroup": "BTP_ADMINS",
        "roleCollection": "Subaccount Administrator"
    },
    {
        "iasGroup": "BTP_DEVELOPERS",
        "roleCollection": "Extension Developer"
    },
    {
        "iasGroup": "CPI_OPERATORS",
        "roleCollection": "PI Business Expert"
    }
]

map-roles.mjs

import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import 'dotenv/config';

const { TOKEN_URL, CLIENT_ID, CLIENT_SECRET, API_URL, IAS_ORIGIN_KEY } = process.env;

async function getToken() {
    const params = new URLSearchParams({
        grant_type: 'client_credentials',
        response_type: 'token',
        client_id: CLIENT_ID,
        client_secret: CLIENT_SECRET
    });
    const res = await fetch(TOKEN_URL, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
        body: params
    });
    const { access_token } = await res.json();
    return access_token;
}

async function mapRoleCollection(token, iasGroup, roleCollection) {
    const url = `${API_URL}/sap/rest/authorization/v2/identity-providers/${IAS_ORIGIN_KEY}/attributes`;
    const res = await fetch(url, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: {
            Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
            'Content-Type': 'application/json',
            Accept: 'application/json'
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({
            attributeName: 'Groups',
            attributeValue: iasGroup,
            operator: 'equals',
            roleCollectionName: roleCollection
        })
    });

    if (res.status === 409) {
        console.log(`Already mapped: "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    if (res.status === 404) {
        console.error(`Not found (check name): "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    if (!res.ok) {
        console.error(`Failed (${res.status}): "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
        return;
    }
    console.log(`Mapped: "${iasGroup}" → "${roleCollection}"`);
}

const mappings = JSON.parse(readFileSync('./mappings.json', 'utf-8'));
const token = await getToken();

for (const { iasGroup, roleCollection } of mappings) {
    await mapRoleCollection(token, iasGroup, roleCollection);
}

Install the one dependency and run:

npm install dotenv
node map-roles.mjs

You'll see a clear log for every mapping: success, already exists, or failure with the exact entry so you can investigate.

Bonus: Multi-Environment Reuse

Once your mappings.json is ready, deploying to multiple environments is trivial. Re-target the BTP CLI and generate a fresh set of credentials for each subaccount:

btp target --subaccount <DEV_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

# update .env, then:
node map-roles.mjs

# next subaccount 
btp target --subaccount <QA_ID>
btp create security/api-credential --name my-credential

# update .env, then:
node map-roles.mjs

# and so on ...

What was an 8-hour cockpit exercise becomes a 2-minute operation per environment. Repeatable, consistent, and auditable.

 

Conclusion

The SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service API is one of those tools that, once you know it's there, you'll reach for regularly. The manual cockpit approach is fine for a handful of mappings, but as soon as you're dealing with real-world project complexity with dozens of role collections, multiple environments, repeated deployments, it simply doesn't scale.

The setup described in this post takes maybe 30 minutes the first time: prepare your mappings.json, configure the .env, run one test call to validate. After that, it's just a matter of running the script. For the customer that inspired this post, what would have been a full day of clicking was done before lunch.

If you give this a try, I'd love to hear how it works for you especially if you adapt the script or extend it to cover other security artifacts. Drop a comment below or reach out directly.

Further Resources

  • Download SAP BTP CLI – https://tools.hana.ondemand.com/#cloud
  • BTP CLI Documentation – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/sap-business-technology-platform/account-administration-using-sap-btp-command-line-interface-btp-cli
  • btp create security/api-credential – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/btp-cli-command-reference/btp-create-security-api-credential
  • SAP Business Accelerator Hub – Authorization API – https://api.sap.com/api/AuthorizationAPI/resource/Role_collections
  • Accessing Administration APIs of SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/sap-business-technology-platform/accessing-administration-using-apis-of-sap-authorization-and-trust-management-service
  • Map Role Collections to User Groups – SAP Help – https://help.sap.com/docs/btp/sap-business-technology-platform/map-role-collections-to-user-groups
